display_name: Fritz Haag Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr Riesling Auslese, Mosel
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr is a blue Devonian slate amphitheater on the Mosel, and that matters because slate stores heat by day and releases it at night, helping Riesling ripen fully at very low alcohol while keeping razor-cut acidity. In Auslese form, this site gives a wine that is rich in extract and fruit concentration but still weightless in feel, which is why bottles like the 2010 and 2011 can sit at 7.0–7.5% ABV and still taste complete rather than diluted.",
  "wine_summary": "This is a benchmark expression of sweet Mosel Riesling from a site that has earned its reputation the hard way: through a combination of steep slope, slate soils, and a cool river-valley climate that lets fruit hang long enough to build Auslese concentration without losing acidity. The wine matters because it sits at the intersection of intensity and lightness. That paradox is the whole point of top Mosel Riesling.\n\nFritz Haag is one of the reference-point names for Brauneberg, and Juffer Sonnenuhr is the estate's calling card. The vineyard's exposure and heat-retentive slate help Riesling achieve full physiological ripeness in a marginal climate, while the Mosel's cool conditions preserve the citrus, green apple, and white peach profile that keeps sweetness from turning heavy. The result is not just a sweet wine; it is a site-driven wine where sugar is only one part of the structure. Acid, low alcohol, and slate-derived mineral tension are doing just as much work.",
  "terroir_expression": "At Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr, the key driver is blue Devonian slate on very steep slopes above the Mosel River. Slate is a metamorphic rock that fractures easily, forcing roots deep while also reflecting and storing heat, which is crucial in a cool region where every degree of ripening matters. That combination pushes the wine toward ripe peach, apricot, lime, and sometimes a smoky-flinty note, but the Mosel climate keeps the fruit lifted rather than tropical. Because the site can ripen grapes while retaining very high acidity, the finished wine tastes sweet yet precise, with a floating texture and a long, stony finish instead of heaviness.",
  "vinification_summary": "Auslese means grapes selected at a higher ripeness level than Kabinett or Spatlese, often with a clear jump in must weight, which is the sugar level in the grape juice before fermentation. For a wine like this, the critical cellar decision is not to ferment to dryness but to stop or naturally end fermentation with substantial residual sugar intact, preserving the Mosel signature of low alcohol and high sweetness balanced by sharp acidity. Specific élevage details are not provided here, so it is safer not to invent them; what matters in the glass is that the winemaking aims to protect purity and site detail rather than add oak or phenolic weight.",
  "food_pairing": "Nashville hot chicken — the residual sugar cools the chile heat, while the wine's acidity cuts through fried crust and keeps the pairing from turning sticky.\nPork schnitzel with lemon and capers — the bright acidity mirrors the lemon, and the sweet-fruit core softens the salt and richness of the fried cutlet.\nThai green curry with shrimp — Riesling's low alcohol and sweetness handle spice better than dry high-alcohol whites, and the lime-peach profile works with coconut, herbs, and shellfish.\nFoie gras with quince — a classic pairing because the wine has enough sugar concentration for the richness, but Mosel acidity keeps the match from feeling dense.\nBlue cheese tart with caramelized onions — salt, fat, and pungency need sweetness and acid together; this wine has both, plus enough delicacy that the pairing still feels precise.",
  "comparable_wines": "Joh. Jos. Prum Wehlener Sonnenuhr Riesling Auslese — comparable for the low-alcohol, high-acid Mosel sweet style, though often even more filigreed and slower to open in youth.\nEgon Muller Scharzhofberger Riesling Spatlese or Auslese — similar in the interplay of sweetness and acidity, but Saar fruit tends to be even more linear and cool-toned.\nMaximin Grunhaus Abtsberg Riesling Auslese — another steep-slope Mosel/Saar-Ruwer reference point where slate and cold climate produce sweet Riesling with very light body and long mineral drive.",
  "style_profile": "Light-bodied sweet white with piercing acidity and slate-driven mineral length",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink young for vivid peach-lime fruit or cellar for 15-30 years if well stored at a cool, stable temperature away from light. Older bottles can gain honey, petrol, and dried citrus complexity without losing lift.",
  "value_assessment": "$45-90 is the realistic retail band for many recent releases and back-vintage bottles, with older or scarcer vintages moving higher. At that level it competes with Joh. Jos. Prum Auslese and Donnhoff Oberhauser Brucke Auslese; this is worth buying when you want classic Mosel sweetness with more site signature than many similarly priced dessert wines. For the category, the value is strong because few wines deliver this level of longevity, complexity, and low-alcohol precision at the same tariff.",
  "market_position": "This is squarely aimed at serious Riesling drinkers, collectors building German wine depth, and restaurant programs that want a real Mosel reference rather than a token sweet wine. It belongs on lists with thoughtful pairing menus, especially where spice, foie gras, or blue cheese appear, and it also works on retail shelves that serve buyers who understand that Auslese is not a beginner's sugar bomb. Casual drinkers can love it, but only if they are open to sweetness as a structural element rather than a flaw.",
  "insider_take": "The tradeoff is simple: if you want dry Riesling, skip this and stop arguing with the label. The designation data around this wine is messy, but Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr Auslese from Fritz Haag is compelling precisely because it leans into the Mosel's sweet-low-alcohol style instead of trying to mimic dry power. What people get wrong is assuming sweetness means heaviness; in top Mosel Auslese, sweetness is carried on acid and slate tension, so the wine drinks lighter than many dry whites.",

parsed.hook: Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr is a blue Devonian slate amphitheater on the Mosel, and that matters because slate stores heat by day and releases it at night, helping Riesling ripen fully at very low alcohol while keeping razor-cut acidity. In Auslese form, this site gives a wine that is rich in extract and fruit concentration but still weightless in feel, which is why bottles like the 2010 and 2011 can sit at 7.0–7.5% ABV and still taste complete rather than diluted.
parsed.wine_summary:
This is a benchmark expression of sweet Mosel Riesling from a site that has earned its reputation the hard way: through a combination of steep slope, slate soils, and a cool river-valley climate that lets fruit hang long enough to build Auslese concentration without losing acidity. The wine matters because it sits at the intersection of intensity and lightness. That paradox is the whole point of top Mosel Riesling.

Fritz Haag is one of the reference-point names for Brauneberg, and Juffer Sonnenuhr is the estate's calling card. The vineyard's exposure and heat-retentive slate help Riesling achieve full physiological ripeness in a marginal climate, while the Mosel's cool conditions preserve the citrus, green apple, and white peach profile that keeps sweetness from turning heavy. The result is not just a sweet wine; it is a site-driven wine where sugar is only one part of the structure. Acid, low alcohol, and slate-derived mineral tension are doing just as much work.
parsed.terroir_expression: At Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr, the key driver is blue Devonian slate on very steep slopes above the Mosel River. Slate is a metamorphic rock that fractures easily, forcing roots deep while also reflecting and storing heat, which is crucial in a cool region where every degree of ripening matters. That combination pushes the wine toward ripe peach, apricot, lime, and sometimes a smoky-flinty note, but the Mosel climate keeps the fruit lifted rather than tropical. Because the site can ripen grapes while retaining very high acidity, the finished wine tastes sweet yet precise, with a floating texture and a long, stony finish instead of heaviness.
parsed.vinification_summary: Auslese means grapes selected at a higher ripeness level than Kabinett or Spatlese, often with a clear jump in must weight, which is the sugar level in the grape juice before fermentation. For a wine like this, the critical cellar decision is not to ferment to dryness but to stop or naturally end fermentation with substantial residual sugar intact, preserving the Mosel signature of low alcohol and high sweetness balanced by sharp acidity. Specific élevage details are not provided here, so it is safer not to invent them; what matters in the glass is that the winemaking aims to protect purity and site detail rather than add oak or phenolic weight.
parsed.food_pairing:
Nashville hot chicken — the residual sugar cools the chile heat, while the wine's acidity cuts through fried crust and keeps the pairing from turning sticky.
Pork schnitzel with lemon and capers — the bright acidity mirrors the lemon, and the sweet-fruit core softens the salt and richness of the fried cutlet.
Thai green curry with shrimp — Riesling's low alcohol and sweetness handle spice better than dry high-alcohol whites, and the lime-peach profile works with coconut, herbs, and shellfish.
Foie gras with quince — a classic pairing because the wine has enough sugar concentration for the richness, but Mosel acidity keeps the match from feeling dense.
Blue cheese tart with caramelized onions — salt, fat, and pungency need sweetness and acid together; this wine has both, plus enough delicacy that the pairing still feels precise.
parsed.comparable_wines:
Joh. Jos. Prum Wehlener Sonnenuhr Riesling Auslese — comparable for the low-alcohol, high-acid Mosel sweet style, though often even more filigreed and slower to open in youth.
Egon Muller Scharzhofberger Riesling Spatlese or Auslese — similar in the interplay of sweetness and acidity, but Saar fruit tends to be even more linear and cool-toned.
Maximin Grunhaus Abtsberg Riesling Auslese — another steep-slope Mosel/Saar-Ruwer reference point where slate and cold climate produce sweet Riesling with very light body and long mineral drive.
parsed.style_profile: Light-bodied sweet white with piercing acidity and slate-driven mineral length
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink young for vivid peach-lime fruit or cellar for 15-30 years if well stored at a cool, stable temperature away from light. Older bottles can gain honey, petrol, and dried citrus complexity without losing lift.
parsed.value_assessment: $45-90 is the realistic retail band for many recent releases and back-vintage bottles, with older or scarcer vintages moving higher. At that level it competes with Joh. Jos. Prum Auslese and Donnhoff Oberhauser Brucke Auslese; this is worth buying when you want classic Mosel sweetness with more site signature than many similarly priced dessert wines. For the category, the value is strong because few wines deliver this level of longevity, complexity, and low-alcohol precision at the same tariff.
parsed.market_position: This is squarely aimed at serious Riesling drinkers, collectors building German wine depth, and restaurant programs that want a real Mosel reference rather than a token sweet wine. It belongs on lists with thoughtful pairing menus, especially where spice, foie gras, or blue cheese appear, and it also works on retail shelves that serve buyers who understand that Auslese is not a beginner's sugar bomb. Casual drinkers can love it, but only if they are open to sweetness as a structural element rather than a flaw.
parsed.insider_take: The tradeoff is simple: if you want dry Riesling, skip this and stop arguing with the label. The designation data around this wine is messy, but Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr Auslese from Fritz Haag is compelling precisely because it leans into the Mosel's sweet-low-alcohol style instead of trying to mimic dry power. What people get wrong is assuming sweetness means heaviness; in top Mosel Auslese, sweetness is carried on acid and slate tension, so the wine drinks lighter than many dry whites.
